title: Business rules (tenant settings) and business-assignment slots backend
objective: Port the tenant business-rules API (high-value threshold, SLA targets, expiry/stall/aging/duplicate thresholds, ref formats, display currency, max attachment MB, pricing-approval gate) and the fixed two-slot business-assignments API (rm/underwriter, one role each) (P-04, section 12 Settings).
scope: GET/PUT business rules endpoints per the reference contract (tenant-scoped, permission-bound, audited)
Validation: thresholds positive, SLA targets sane ranges, ref-format templates valid (tokens per reference), display currency ISO code, max attachment MB bounded, toggle types
Business assignments: GET/PUT the two fixed slots — each maps to exactly one role per tenant; no applies_to lists; assignment changes audited
Settings consumed downstream (leads/quotes/jobs) exposed through a typed settings reader service

T-016 CONTRACT EXTENDED, NOT CONTRADICTED: tenants/service.ts provisions the tenant_settings row from column defaults only. This task reads and updates that same row and never creates one - a missing row stays a 404 (BUSINESS_RULES_NOT_FOUND), matching the reference, which calls it a provisioning alarm rather than a caller error. The suite provisions its fixture tenants exactly as tenants/service.ts does, so the defaults assertion tests the MIGRATION rather than the fixture.

MISSING-ROW SEMANTICS DIVERGE FROM THE TASK FILE'S WORDING, DELIBERATELY: test_plan.unit suggested 'missing row -> defaults'. The reference (TenantSettingsProvider.cs:24-25) THROWS instead, and that is what getTenantSettings does. A defaults fallback would let a tenant whose provisioning silently failed keep running on different thresholds from the ones its Settings screen reports (which 404s) - a data-correctness bug wearing a working system's clothes. DEFAULT_TENANT_SETTINGS is exported and asserted against a real provisioned row, but deliberately NOT wired as a fallback. FLAGGED as a decision made without explicit guidance.

SETTINGS READER DOES NO CROSS-REQUEST CACHING (N-02): the reference cached per request scope, which has no Vercel equivalent - a module-level cache would outlive the request on a warm function instance and serve one tenant's thresholds to the next.

SHARED REFERENCE-FORMAT GRAMMAR: business-rules/reference-format.ts is the single module for the {YYYY}/{SEQ:n} template grammar, exported for T-024's lead/quote reference generator. The validator and the renderer MUST agree - a template accepted at settings-save time but unrenderable would fail at every subsequent lead insert, surfacing in a different feature from the one that caused it. The unit suite renders every template it accepts, for exactly that reason.

The eligible reader canNOT use forTenant(): users, user_roles, user_permissions, user_groups, group_members, group_roles and group_permissions are global/unpartitioned. Four carry a NULLABLE tenant_id (a grant may be global or tenant-scoped) and three carry none at all - group_roles and group_permissions inherit tenant scope from the owning group, so their predicate is written against user_groups.tenant_id. Every predicate is therefore explicit, exactly as rbac/admin-repository.ts documents, and with RLS not adopted (spec Q-10) there is nothing beneath them. M15 and M17 are the tests that make that safe rather than merely intended.

reference_parity_notes: ReferenceFormatTemplate's doc comment says a template must contain EXACTLY ONE {SEQ:n} token; its CODE uses Any(...) (at least one). The CODE is preserved as the contract - tightening it would 422 a template a tenant may already have stored. Pinned by a unit test.

BUSINESS_ASSIGNMENTS_NOT_FOUND (404) is declared by the reference mapper but emitted by NO handler: an unconfigured slot is null, not an error, and that is the normal state of every freshly created tenant. The constant is exported for documentation but has no constructor, so no handler can start emitting a 404 the SPA has never had to handle.

Currency validation is SHAPE-ONLY (three uppercase letters), not the ISO-4217 registry - the reference validator's own comment calls this an explicit scope boundary. 'ZZZ' is accepted by both; a test pins it so a later 'improvement' cannot silently reject codes an existing tenant already stores.

tenant_settings.expire_lead_when_last_quote_expires is NOT on the wire (the reference DTO omits it and the write shape does not accept it). It is exposed only to server-side consumers through getTenantSettings, whose return type is deliberately separate from BusinessRulesDto so a consumer cannot reach it by widening the wire DTO.

Unknown body keys: STRIPPED on business-rules (C# record binding ignores them, and there is nothing to smuggle since the update writes 21 named columns) but REJECTED on business-assignments (there an unknown key IS the attempted third slot, and stripping it would answer 200 to a request that did nothing). The asymmetry is deliberate and documented in both schema files.
toBusinessRulesDto is an EXPLICIT 21-field projection rather than a spread-with-omit, so a column added by a later migration cannot silently widen the wire contract (spec A-3).

A missing X-Tenant-Id answers 403 with the uniform denial message, not 400 - the tenancy middleware makes missing/malformed/nonexistent/non-member indistinguishable to prevent tenant enumeration. Measured, after an initial assumption of 400 was proven wrong by a failing test.

Audit entity_id is the TENANT ID on both endpoints (matching the reference): there is exactly one settings row per tenant, and a slot replace may create, update and delete rows at once, so the tenant is the identity of the changed configuration.

Both mutations audit inside the SAME transaction as the write, which is strictly stronger than the reference (it wrote the audit row after SaveChangesAsync, so a crash in between changed a tenant's SLA targets - or repointed who owns every lead - with no record of who did it).

PORTED ASYMMETRY, FLAGGED: GetUsersHoldingRoleAsync does NOT check the role's own is_active (EligibleAssigneeReader.cs:28-40), while GetUsersHoldingPermissionAsync checks r.IsActive on every path (:57,:70). So a role deactivated AFTER being configured into a slot still yields its holders in the picker. Only reachable by deactivating an already-slotted role (the slot PUT rejects inactive roles). Preserved rather than silently tightened - tightening it would empty a tenant's Assign dialog with no error to explain why. Documented in eligible-repository.ts.

The reference's `.Distinct()` (:112) is a no-op in the ported query shape, because the candidate set is applied as an `IN (subquery)` rather than a JOIN, which cannot duplicate a users row. Deliberately not reproduced as a keyword; instead the OUTCOME ('returns each eligible user ONCE when several grant paths apply') is pinned by a test for both routes, so a future rewrite that reintroduces a join must keep it true.

`%` and `_` inside a search term keep their LIKE-wildcard meaning, exactly as the reference's `$"%{search.Trim()}%"` did. Preserved quirk, not an injection risk - the term is a bound parameter throughout.

eligible-users answers 400 (not 422, not 404) for a missing or unparseable assignmentId, because `long assignmentId` is a REQUIRED minimal-API query binding and fails model binding before the handler runs. Deliberately not routed through the domain's *_VALIDATION_FAILED mapper, which would report the wrong class of failure.
